claim: Organ function declines with age.
source: Organ function declines with age, and large-scale transcriptomic analyses have highlighted differential aging trajectories across tissues.
evidence: This is a general statement supported by established scientific consensus and cited literature in the introduction.

claim: Large-scale transcriptomic analyses have highlighted differential aging trajectories across tissues.
source: Organ function declines with age, and large-scale transcriptomic analyses have highlighted differential aging trajectories across tissues.
evidence: This statement references prior transcriptomic studies on aging.

claim: The mechanism underlying shared and organ-selective functional changes across the lifespan remains poorly understood.
source: The mechanism underlying shared and organ-selective functional changes across the lifespan, however, still remains poorly understood.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Mitochondria play a central role in powering cellular processes needed to maintain tissue health.
source: Given the central role of mitochondria in powering cellular processes needed to maintain tissue health, we therefore undertook a systematic assessment of respiratory activity across 33 different tissues in young (2.5 months) and old (20 months) mice of both sexes.
evidence: This is established scientific knowledge about mitochondrial function.

claim: The study assessed respiratory activity across 33 different tissues in young (2.5 months) and old (20 months) mice of both sexes.
source: Given the central role of mitochondria in powering cellular processes needed to maintain tissue health, we therefore undertook a systematic assessment of respiratory activity across 33 different tissues in young (2.5 months) and old (20 months) mice of both sexes.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: Within any group of mice, mitochondrial activity varies widely across tissues, with the highest values consistently seen in heart, brown fat, and kidney.
source: Our high-resolution mitochondrial respiration atlas reveals: (1) within any group of mice, mitochondrial activity varies widely across tissues, with the highest values consistently seen in heart, brown fat, and kidney;
evidence: This is a primary finding from the respirometry data presented in the study.

claim: Biological sex is a significant but minor contributor to mitochondrial respiration.
source: (2) biological sex is a significant but minor contributor to mitochondrial respiration, and its contributions are tissue-specific, with major differences seen in the pancreas, stomach, and white adipose tissue;
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from statistical analysis of the respirometry data.

claim: Sex contributions to mitochondrial respiration are tissue-specific, with major differences seen in the pancreas, stomach, and white adipose tissue.
source: (2) biological sex is a significant but minor contributor to mitochondrial respiration, and its contributions are tissue-specific, with major differences seen in the pancreas, stomach, and white adipose tissue;
evidence: This is based on tissue-by-tissue comparison of respirometry data between sexes.

claim: Age is a dominant factor affecting mitochondrial activity, especially across most brain regions, different fat depots, skeletal muscle groups, eyes, and different regions of the gastrointestinal tract.
source: (3) age is a dominant factor affecting mitochondrial activity, especially across most brain regions, different fat depots, skeletal muscle groups, eyes, and different regions of the gastrointestinal tract;
evidence: This is a primary finding from comparing young and old mice across tissues.

claim: Age effects on mitochondrial activity can be sex- and tissue-specific, with some of the largest effects seen in pancreas, heart, adipose tissue, and skeletal muscle.
source: (4) age effects can be sex- and tissue-specific, with some of the largest effects seen in pancreas, heart, adipose tissue, and skeletal muscle;
evidence: This is based on analysis of age-by-sex interactions in the respirometry data.

claim: While aging alters the functional trajectories of mitochondria in a majority of tissues, some are remarkably resilient to age-induced changes.
source: (5) while aging alters the functional trajectories of mitochondria in a majority of tissues, some are remarkably resilient to age-induced changes.
evidence: This is an observation from the respirometry data showing differential responses to aging.

claim: The data provide the most comprehensive compendium of mitochondrial respiration across diverse tissues and organ systems.
source: Altogether, our data provide the most comprehensive compendium of mitochondrial respiration and illuminate functional signatures of aging across diverse tissues and organ systems.
evidence: This is a claim about the scope and novelty of the dataset.

claim: Age is one of the most significant contributors to disease risk.
source: Age is one of the most significant contributors to disease risk (Kennedy et al., 2014), and the aging process is influenced by a variety of genetic and environmental factors at the tissue and organismal level (Tian et al., 2023; Nie et al., 2022; Kuo et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Kennedy et al., 2014.

claim: The aging process is influenced by a variety of genetic and environmental factors at the tissue and organismal level.
source: Age is one of the most significant contributors to disease risk (Kennedy et al., 2014), and the aging process is influenced by a variety of genetic and environmental factors at the tissue and organismal level (Tian et al., 2023; Nie et al., 2022; Kuo et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Tian et al., 2023; Nie et al., 2022; Kuo et al., 2022.

claim: Bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analyses of mouse tissues across the lifespan have shown that aging tempo and trajectory varies widely across tissues.
source: Bulk and single-cell transcriptomic analyses of mouse tissues across the lifespan have shown that aging tempo and trajectory, as indicated by tissue transcriptomic signatures, varies widely across tissues (Schaum et al., 2020; Zhang et al., 2021; Almanzar et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to transcriptomic studies.

claim: Many of the transcriptomic signatures of aging across tissues can be significantly reversed by caloric restriction or rejuvenated by the transfusion of young blood.
source: Remarkably, many of the transcriptomic signatures of aging across tissues can be significantly reversed by caloric restriction or rejuvenated by the transfusion of young blood (Pálovics et al., 2022; Ma et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Pálovics et al., 2022 and Ma et al., 2020.

claim: Large-scale proteomic analyses of human plasma reveal distinct waves of changes across the lifespan, which are associated with distinct biological pathways and affect age-related phenotypic traits and diseases.
source: Large-scale proteomic analyses of human plasma also reveal distinct waves of changes across the lifespan, which are associated with distinct biological pathways and affect age-related phenotypic traits and diseases (Lehallier et al., 2019; Oh et al., 2023).
evidence: This is supported by citations to proteomic studies.

claim: There is no consensus regarding the mechanisms underlying aging at the cellular or tissue level.
source: Despite enormous progress, there is no consensus regarding the mechanisms underlying aging at the cellular or tissue level.
evidence: This is an assessment of the current state of the field.

claim: It remains a major challenge to distinguish between the driver and passenger mechanisms of aging.
source: Although many non-mutually exclusive hypotheses have been put forth to explain the root cause of aging - oxidative damage, genomic instability, epigenetic changes, loss of proteostasis, mitochondrial dysfunction, DNA damage, telomere shortening, cellular senescence, stem cell exhaustion - it remains a major challenge to distinguish between the driver and passenger mechanisms of aging (de Magalhães, 2024).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to de Magalhães, 2024.

claim: Mitochondria play an important role in the aging process.
source: In the present study, we focused on aging from a mitochondrial perspective, as this organelle is known to play an important role in the aging process (Jang et al., 2018; Lima et al., 2022; Lanza and Nair, 2010; Sun et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Mitochondria supply the bulk of the energy needed to maintain tissue health and repair tissue damage.
source: Mitochondria supply the bulk of the energy needed to maintain tissue health and repair tissue damage, and their function tends to decline with age.
evidence: This is established knowledge about mitochondrial function.

claim: Mitochondrial function tends to decline with age.
source: Mitochondria supply the bulk of the energy needed to maintain tissue health and repair tissue damage, and their function tends to decline with age.
evidence: This is a general observation about aging and mitochondria.

claim: Over time, damage accumulates in mitochondrial DNA, proteins, and lipids, which compromises their functional integrity and leads to dysregulated metabolism and increased oxidative stress.
source: Over time, damage accumulates in mitochondrial DNA, proteins, and lipids, which compromises their functional integrity and leads to dysregulated metabolism and increased oxidative stress.
evidence: This describes a mechanism of mitochondrial aging based on established knowledge.

claim: Recent transcriptomic analyses have highlighted major reductions in electron transport chain gene expression across the lifespan.
source: Recent transcriptomic analyses have highlighted major reductions in electron transport chain gene expression across the lifespan (Schaum et al., 2020), and these changes can be significantly reversed by the transfusion of young blood into older mice (Pálovics et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by citations to transcriptomic studies.

claim: Changes in electron transport chain gene expression can be significantly reversed by the transfusion of young blood into older mice.
source: Recent transcriptomic analyses have highlighted major reductions in electron transport chain gene expression across the lifespan (Schaum et al., 2020), and these changes can be significantly reversed by the transfusion of young blood into older mice (Pálovics et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Pálovics et al., 2022.

claim: Aging-associated reduction in mitochondrial OXPHOS gene expression appears to be conserved between human, mouse, fly, and worm.
source: Aging-associated reduction in mitochondrial OXPHOS gene expression appears to be conserved between human, mouse, fly, and worm (Zahn et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Zahn et al., 2007.

claim: Mitochondrial dysfunction has been implicated in various age-related diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders, cardiovascular diseases, and metabolic syndromes.
source: Accordingly, mitochondrial dysfunction has been implicated in various age-related diseases, including neurodegenerative disorders, cardiovascular diseases, and metabolic syndromes (Haas, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Haas, 2019.

claim: Boosting mitochondrial health has been shown to delay age-related decline in organ function.
source: Boosting mitochondrial health has been shown to delay age-related decline in organ function (Foote et al., 2018; Lima et al., 2023; Chiao et al., 2020; Nilsson and Tarnopolsky, 2019).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: An innovative method by Acin-Perez and coworkers has made it possible to assess mitochondrial function in previously frozen tissues.
source: This barrier, however, has been recently overcome. An innovative method by Acin-Perez and coworkers has made it possible to now assess mitochondrial function in previously frozen tissues (Acin-Perez et al., 2020).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Acin-Perez et al., 2020.

claim: The new method circumvents the need to isolate mitochondria at the time of tissue harvest, allowing many tissues to be collected, frozen, and assayed at a later time.
source: This new method circumvents the need to isolate mitochondria at the time of tissue harvest, allowing many tissues to be collected, frozen, and assayed at a later time.
evidence: This describes the advantage of the Acin-Perez method.

claim: The dataset consists of a total of 1320 tissue samples from 40 mice and 3960 high-resolution respirometry assays encompassing three technical replicates.
source: The dataset consists of a total of 1320 tissue samples from 40 mice and 3960 high-resolution respirometry assays encompassing three technical replicates.
evidence: This describes the scale of the experimental dataset.

claim: This study represents the largest and the most comprehensive tissue respirometry analysis to date.
source: Our study represents the largest and the most comprehensive tissue respirometry analysis to date.
evidence: This is a claim about the novelty and scope of the study.

claim: 33 tissues were collected from young (2.5 months) or old (20 months) male or female mice (n=10 mice per age and sex).
source: To assay mitochondrial respiration and its maintenance across age and sex, we collected 33 tissues from young (2.5 months; ~18-year-equivalent in human) or old (20 months; ~65-year-equivalent in human) male or female mice (n=10 mice per age and sex).
evidence: This describes the experimental design.

claim: Young mice (2.5 months) are approximately 18-year-equivalent in human.
source: To assay mitochondrial respiration and its maintenance across age and sex, we collected 33 tissues from young (2.5 months; ~18-year-equivalent in human) or old (20 months; ~65-year-equivalent in human) male or female mice (n=10 mice per age and sex).
evidence: This provides a human age equivalence for the young mouse age.

claim: Old mice (20 months) are approximately 65-year-equivalent in human.
source: To assay mitochondrial respiration and its maintenance across age and sex, we collected 33 tissues from young (2.5 months; ~18-year-equivalent in human) or old (20 months; ~65-year-equivalent in human) male or female mice (n=10 mice per age and sex).
evidence: This provides a human age equivalence for the old mouse age.

claim: Young male and young female mice have the greatest oxygen consumption in the heart atria and ventricles, brown adipose tissue (BAT), kidney cortex and medulla.
source: Ranking young male or young female tissues by their respiration via CI (NADH-stimulated), CII (succinate-stimulated), or CIV (TMPD and ascorbate-stimulated) showed that both sexes have the greatest oxygen consumption in the heart atria and ventricles, brown adipose tissue (BAT), kidney cortex and medulla, and the lowest respiration in the colon (distal or proximal), plantaris muscle, jejunum, ileum, and mesenteric white adipose tissue (mesWAT) (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is based on ranking of respirometry data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Young male and young female mice have the lowest respiration in the colon (distal or proximal), plantaris muscle, jejunum, ileum, and mesenteric white adipose tissue (mesWAT).
source: Ranking young male or young female tissues by their respiration via CI (NADH-stimulated), CII (succinate-stimulated), or CIV (TMPD and ascorbate-stimulated) showed that both sexes have the greatest oxygen consumption in the heart atria and ventricles, brown adipose tissue (BAT), kidney cortex and medulla, and the lowest respiration in the colon (distal or proximal), plantaris muscle, jejunum, ileum, and mesenteric white adipose tissue (mesWAT) (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is based on ranking of respirometry data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Old male mice have the highest oxygen consumption in the heart atria and ventricles, BAT, diaphragm muscle, kidney cortex, and medulla.
source: Ranking old male tissues by their respiration via CI, CII, or CIV showed that the heart atria and ventricles, BAT, diaphragm muscle, kidney cortex, and medulla have the highest oxygen consumption, while the ileum, pancreas, skin, duodenum, stomach, distal colon, mesWAT, and inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT) have the lowest (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on ranking of respirometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Old male mice have the lowest respiration in the ileum, pancreas, skin, duodenum, stomach, distal colon, mesWAT, and inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT).
source: Ranking old male tissues by their respiration via CI, CII, or CIV showed that the heart atria and ventricles, BAT, diaphragm muscle, kidney cortex, and medulla have the highest oxygen consumption, while the ileum, pancreas, skin, duodenum, stomach, distal colon, mesWAT, and inguinal white adipose tissue (iWAT) have the lowest (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is based on ranking of respirometry data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Old female mice have the highest respiration in the heart atria and ventricles, BAT, kidney cortex, and diaphragm.
source: Ranking all old female tissues by their respiration via CI, CII, or CIV showed that the heart atria and ventricles, BAT, kidney cortex, and diaphragm have the highest respiration, while the pancreas, duodenum, mesWAT, ileum, distal colon, eyes, and skin have the lowest (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on ranking of respirometry data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Old female mice have the lowest respiration in the pancreas, duodenum, mesWAT, ileum, distal colon, eyes, and skin.
source: Ranking all old female tissues by their respiration via CI, CII, or CIV showed that the heart atria and ventricles, BAT, kidney cortex, and diaphragm have the highest respiration, while the pancreas, duodenum, mesWAT, ileum, distal colon, eyes, and skin have the lowest (Figure 2D).
evidence: This is based on ranking of respirometry data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Even when age and sex are controlled for, mitochondria within a single tissue-classification or organ system can have distinct respiration signatures.
source: Remarkably, even when age and sex are controlled for, mitochondria within a single tissue-classification or organ system can have distinct respiration signatures.
evidence: This is an observation from the data showing heterogeneity within tissue types.

claim: Young male and female mice have similar distributions in oxygen consumption rate across 32 tissues.
source: A systems-level view of mitochondrial respiration via CI, CII, or CIV across 32 tissues (omitting reproductive tissues) showed that young male and female mice have similar distributions in oxygen consumption rate (OCR; Figure 3A–C, left panel).
evidence: This is based on comparison of OCR distributions shown in Figure 3A-C.

claim: Individual tissue-level analysis of respiration through CI showed only two significant differences between young male and female mice, in the quadriceps muscle complex and gonadal white adipose tissue (gWAT).
source: Individual tissue-level analysis of respiration through CI showed only two significant differences between young male and female mice, in the quadriceps muscle complex and gonadal white adipose tissue (gWAT) (Figure 3A, right panel).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CI respiration data shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Young males have higher mitochondrial respiration through CII in the kidney medulla, stomach, quadriceps muscle complex, hippocampus, and gastrocnemius muscle compared to young females.
source: Individual tissue comparisons of respiration through CII showed that young males have higher mitochondrial respiration in the kidney medulla, stomach, quadriceps muscle complex, hippocampus, and gastrocnemius muscle, and reduced mitochondrial activity in gWAT and ileum relative to young females (Figure 3B, right panel).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CII respiration data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Young males have reduced mitochondrial activity through CII in gWAT and ileum relative to young females.
source: Individual tissue comparisons of respiration through CII showed that young males have higher mitochondrial respiration in the kidney medulla, stomach, quadriceps muscle complex, hippocampus, and gastrocnemius muscle, and reduced mitochondrial activity in gWAT and ileum relative to young females (Figure 3B, right panel).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CII respiration data shown in Figure 3B.

claim: Young males have higher mitochondrial activity at CIV in the BAT, heart ventricles, kidney medulla, hippocampus, stomach, quadriceps muscle complex, and gastrocnemius muscle compared to young females.
source: Respiration at CIV showed that young males have higher mitochondrial activity in the BAT, heart ventricles, kidney medulla, hippocampus, stomach, quadriceps muscle complex, and gastrocnemius muscle and reduced mitochondrial activity in the gWAT and duodenum when compared to young females (Figure 3C, right panel).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CIV respiration data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Young males have reduced mitochondrial activity at CIV in the gWAT and duodenum when compared to young females.
source: Respiration at CIV showed that young males have higher mitochondrial activity in the BAT, heart ventricles, kidney medulla, hippocampus, stomach, quadriceps muscle complex, and gastrocnemius muscle and reduced mitochondrial activity in the gWAT and duodenum when compared to young females (Figure 3C, right panel).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CIV respiration data shown in Figure 3C.

claim: Young males have higher mitochondrial respiration in the stomach, kidney, and skeletal muscle, whereas young females have higher mitochondrial respiration in the GI tract and different fat depots (gWAT and mesWAT).
source: A relative and global view of the sex-specific differences across young male and female mice showed that males have higher mitochondrial respiration in the stomach, kidney, and skeletal muscle, whereas females have higher mitochondrial respiration in the GI tract and different fat depots (gWAT and mesWAT) (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is based on heat map analysis shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Old and young male mice have similar distributions of OCR across all 33 tissues.
source: A systems-level view of respiration via CI, CII, or CIV across all 33 tissues showed that old and young male mice have similar distributions of OCR (Figure 4A–C, left panel).
evidence: This is based on comparison of OCR distributions shown in Figure 4A-C.

claim: Old males showed a striking increase in mitochondrial activity via CI in the heart atria, skeletal muscles (diaphragm, soleus, tongue, plantaris, gastrocnemius), testis, mesWAT, and ileum relative to young males.
source: Old males showed a striking increase in mitochondrial activity via CI in the heart atria, skeletal muscles (diaphragm, soleus, tongue, plantaris, gastrocnemius), testis, mesWAT, and ileum, and reduced mitochondrial respiration in the brain cortex, cerebellum, hippocampus, liver, eyes, skin, iWAT, BAT, and stomach relative to young males (Figure 4A, right panel).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CI respiration data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Old males showed reduced mitochondrial respiration via CI in the brain cortex, cerebellum, hippocampus, liver, eyes, skin, iWAT, BAT, and stomach relative to young males.
source: Old males showed a striking increase in mitochondrial activity via CI in the heart atria, skeletal muscles (diaphragm, soleus, tongue, plantaris, gastrocnemius), testis, mesWAT, and ileum, and reduced mitochondrial respiration in the brain cortex, cerebellum, hippocampus, liver, eyes, skin, iWAT, BAT, and stomach relative to young males (Figure 4A, right panel).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CI respiration data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Old males have markedly higher mitochondrial activity through CII in the heart ventricles, skeletal muscles (diaphragm and plantaris), jejunum, ileum, and mesWAT when compared to young males.
source: Viewing respiration through CII also showed that old males have markedly higher mitochondrial activity in the heart ventricles, skeletal muscles (diaphragm and plantaris), jejunum, ileum, and mesWAT when compared to young males (Figure 4B, right panel).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CII respiration data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Old males had reduced mitochondrial activity via CII in the brain (cortex and hippocampus), BAT, stomach, quadriceps muscle complex, liver, and eyes when compared to young males.
source: In contrast, old males had reduced mitochondrial activity via CII in the brain (cortex and hippocampus), BAT, stomach, quadriceps muscle complex, liver, and eyes when compared to young males.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CII respiration data.

claim: Old males have markedly elevated mitochondrial activity at CIV in the skeletal muscle (diaphragm, soleus, plantaris), ileum, and cecum relative to young males.
source: Respiration at CIV showed that old males have markedly elevated mitochondrial activity in the skeletal muscle (diaphragm, soleus, plantaris), ileum, and cecum, and reduced mitochondrial activity in the brain (cortex, cerebellum, hippocampus), BAT, liver, spleen, eyes, quadriceps muscle complex, pancreas, duodenum, stomach, and iWAT, relative to young males (Figure 4C, right panel).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CIV respiration data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Old males have reduced mitochondrial activity at CIV in the brain (cortex, cerebellum, hippocampus), BAT, liver, spleen, eyes, quadriceps muscle complex, pancreas, duodenum, stomach, and iWAT, relative to young males.
source: Respiration at CIV showed that old males have markedly elevated mitochondrial activity in the skeletal muscle (diaphragm, soleus, plantaris), ileum, and cecum, and reduced mitochondrial activity in the brain (cortex, cerebellum, hippocampus), BAT, liver, spleen, eyes, quadriceps muscle complex, pancreas, duodenum, stomach, and iWAT, relative to young males (Figure 4C, right panel).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CIV respiration data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Old males have significantly elevated mitochondrial activity in the skeletal muscles, mesWAT, GI tract, and heart, with a concomitant reduction in mitochondrial activity in the stomach, iWAT, gWAT, BAT, eyes, and nearly all brain regions compared to young males.
source: A relative and global view of the age-specific differences across male mice showed that old males have significantly elevated mitochondrial activity in the skeletal muscles, mesWAT, GI tract, and heart, with a concomitant reduction in mitochondrial activity in the stomach, iWAT, gWAT, BAT, eyes, and nearly all brain regions (Figure 4D).
evidence: This is based on heat map analysis shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Age has a strong effect in modulating mitochondrial respiration in male mice.
source: Together, these data indicate age has a strong effect in modulating mitochondrial respiration in male mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the age comparison data in males.

claim: Old and young female mice have a similar OCR distribution across all 33 tissues.
source: Systems-level analysis of respiration via CI, CII, or CIV across all 33 tissues showed a similar OCR distribution between old and young female mice (Figure 5A–C, left panel).
evidence: This is based on comparison of OCR distributions shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Old females have elevated mitochondrial activity via CI in the heart ventricles, skeletal muscles (diaphragm, soleus, tongue, and plantaris), and mesWAT compared to young females.
source: Respiration through CI showed that old females have elevated mitochondrial activity in the heart ventricles, skeletal muscles (diaphragm, soleus, tongue, and plantaris), and mesWAT, and a concomitant reduction in mitochondrial activity in the BAT, kidney cortex, brain (cortex and cerebellum), gWAT, iWAT, eyes, and distal colon when compared to young females (Figure 5A, right panel).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CI respiration data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Old females have a reduction in mitochondrial activity via CI in the BAT, kidney cortex, brain (cortex and cerebellum), gWAT, iWAT, eyes, and distal colon when compared to young females.
source: Respiration through CI showed that old females have elevated mitochondrial activity in the heart ventricles, skeletal muscles (diaphragm, soleus, tongue, and plantaris), and mesWAT, and a concomitant reduction in mitochondrial activity in the BAT, kidney cortex, brain (cortex and cerebellum), gWAT, iWAT, eyes, and distal colon when compared to young females (Figure 5A, right panel).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CI respiration data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Old females have increased mitochondrial respiration through CII in skeletal muscles (diaphragm and plantaris), and mesWAT relative to young females.
source: Respiration through CII also showed that old females have increased mitochondrial respiration in skeletal muscles (diaphragm and plantaris), and mesWAT relative to young females (Figure 5B, right panel).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CII respiration data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Old females had reduced mitochondrial respiration via CII in the liver, brain (cortex and cerebellum), gWAT, fallopian tubes, eyes, skin, BAT, heart atria, and pancreas when compared to young females.
source: In contrast, old females had reduced mitochondrial respiration via CII in the liver, brain (cortex and cerebellum), gWAT, fallopian tubes, eyes, skin, BAT, heart atria, and pancreas when compared to young females.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CII respiration data.

claim: Old females have elevated mitochondrial activity at CIV in the skeletal muscle (diaphragm, plantaris, and soleus) and mesWAT relative to young females.
source: Respiration at CIV likewise showed that old females have elevated mitochondrial activity in the skeletal muscle (diaphragm, plantaris, and soleus) and mesWAT relative to young females; concomitantly, old females had reduced mitochondrial activity in the heart atria, brain (cortex and cerebellum), liver, stomach, lung, eyes, jejunum, duodenum, pancreas, and skin when compared to young females (Figure 5C, right panel).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CIV respiration data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Old females had reduced mitochondrial activity at CIV in the heart atria, brain (cortex and cerebellum), liver, stomach, lung, eyes, jejunum, duodenum, pancreas, and skin when compared to young females.
source: Respiration at CIV likewise showed that old females have elevated mitochondrial activity in the skeletal muscle (diaphragm, plantaris, and soleus) and mesWAT relative to young females; concomitantly, old females had reduced mitochondrial activity in the heart atria, brain (cortex and cerebellum), liver, stomach, lung, eyes, jejunum, duodenum, pancreas, and skin when compared to young females (Figure 5C, right panel).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CIV respiration data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Old females have elevated mitochondrial respiration in the skeletal muscles, mesenteric fat, and heart ventricles, and a concomitant reduction in mitochondrial activity in the eyes, skin, duodenum, gWAT, iWAT, BAT, and nearly all brain regions when compared to young females.
source: A relative and global view of the age-specific differences across female mice showed that old females have elevated mitochondrial respiration in the skeletal muscles, mesenteric fat, and heart ventricles, and a concomitant reduction in mitochondrial activity in the eyes, skin, duodenum, gWAT, iWAT, BAT, and nearly all brain regions when compared to young females.
evidence: This is based on analysis of age-related changes in females.

claim: Age has a strong effect in modulating mitochondrial activity in female mice.
source: Similar to males, these data also indicate age has a strong effect in modulating mitochondrial activity in female mice.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the age comparison data in females.

claim: Old male and female mice show no differences in OCR distribution across sex across all 33 tissues.
source: A systems-level view of respiration through CI, CII, or CIV across all 33 tissues showed no differences in OCR distribution across sex in old mice (Figure 6A–C, left panel).
evidence: This is based on comparison of OCR distributions shown in Figure 6A-C.

claim: Old male mice had greater mitochondrial activity via CI in the heart atria, kidney (medulla and cortex), lung, and ileum compared to old females.
source: At the individual tissue level, however, old male mice had greater mitochondrial activity via CI in the heart atria, kidney (medulla and cortex), lung, and ileum, and lower respiration in the BAT and stomach as compared to old females.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CI respiration data in old mice.

claim: Old male mice had lower respiration via CI in the BAT and stomach as compared to old females.
source: At the individual tissue level, however, old male mice had greater mitochondrial activity via CI in the heart atria, kidney (medulla and cortex), lung, and ileum, and lower respiration in the BAT and stomach as compared to old females.
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CI respiration data in old mice.

claim: Old males have higher mitochondrial activity through CII in the kidney (cortex and medulla), lung, and pancreas compared to old females.
source: Respiration through CII showed that old males have higher mitochondrial activity in the kidney (cortex and medulla), lung, and pancreas, and reduced mitochondrial activity in the stomach, relative to old females (Figure 6B, right panel).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CII respiration data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Old males have reduced mitochondrial activity through CII in the stomach, relative to old females.
source: Respiration through CII showed that old males have higher mitochondrial activity in the kidney (cortex and medulla), lung, and pancreas, and reduced mitochondrial activity in the stomach, relative to old females (Figure 6B, right panel).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CII respiration data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Old males have higher mitochondrial respiration at CIV in the heart atria, kidney medulla, soleus muscle, lungs, and eyes compared to old females.
source: Respiration at CIV showed that old males have higher mitochondrial respiration in the heart atria, kidney medulla, soleus muscle, lungs, and eyes, and reduced mitochondrial activity in the cerebellum, iWAT, and mesWAT, when compared to old females (Figure 6C, right panel).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CIV respiration data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Old males have reduced mitochondrial activity at CIV in the cerebellum, iWAT, and mesWAT, when compared to old females.
source: Respiration at CIV showed that old males have higher mitochondrial respiration in the heart atria, kidney medulla, soleus muscle, lungs, and eyes, and reduced mitochondrial activity in the cerebellum, iWAT, and mesWAT, when compared to old females (Figure 6C, right panel).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of CIV respiration data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Old males have elevated mitochondrial activity in the distal colon, lung, eyes, pancreas, soleus, kidney, and heart when compared to old females.
source: A global and relative view of the sex-specific differences across age showed that old males have elevated mitochondrial activity in the distal colon, lung, eyes, pancreas, soleus, kidney, and heart when compared to old females, whereas old females have higher mitochondrial activity in all adipose tissue depots, stomach, and nearly all brain regions when compared to old males (Figure 6D).
evidence: This is based on heat map analysis shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Old females have higher mitochondrial activity in all adipose tissue depots, stomach, and nearly all brain regions when compared to old males.

source: Although sex is a significant biological variable influencing many aspects of physiology and pathophysiology (Mauvais-Jarvis et al., 2020; Austad and Fischer, 2016), and sex hormones are known to affect mitochondrial function (Klinge, 2020; Gaignard et al., 2017; Sultanova et al., 2020), we were surprised that sex has a relatively modest impact on respiratory capacity in mitochondria across tissues and age.

claim: This variability in magnitude of change is consistent with the heterogenous rate of aging across tissues.

claim: Aging induces a reduction in mitochondrial OXPHOS gene expression.

claim: Reduction in mitochondrial OXPHOS gene expression likely is one of the mechanisms that contributes to the reduced mitochondrial activity observed across many tissues in old mice.

claim: Increased mitochondrial respiration is seen in both the oxidative (diaphragm, soleus, tongue) and glycolytic (plantaris) muscle fibers.

claim: Skeletal muscle mass is known to decrease with age.
source: Skeletal muscle mass is known to decrease with age (Wilkinson et al., 2018), and it is frequently but not always accompanied by a reduction in skeletal muscle mitochondrial function in vivo (Gouspillou et al., 2014; Short et al., 2005; Conley et al., 2000; Kent-Braun and Ng, 2000; Chilibeck et al., 1998) and in vitro (Short et al., 2005; Mansouri et al., 2006; Kumaran et al., 2005; Tonkonogi et al., 2003; Drew et al., 2003; Picard et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

evidence: This is supported by citations to prior studies.

claim: Skeletal muscle mitochondrial number increases, whereas mitochondrial size decreases, with age.
source: It has been shown that skeletal muscle mitochondrial number increases, whereas mitochondrial size decreases, with age (Del Campo et al., 2018).

claim: The ultrastructure of mitochondria may change with age.

claim: The heart experiences functional decline with age, and this is thought to be attributed to multiple mechanisms including age-dependent changes in mitochondrial content, morphology, lipid composition, dynamics, activity of the electron transport chain, ROS generation, and susceptibility to mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening.
source: Similar to skeletal muscle, the heart also experiences functional decline with age, and this is thought to be attributed to multiple mechanisms that include age-dependent changes in mitochondrial content, morphology, lipid composition (e.g. cardiolipin) and dynamics (e.g. fusion and fission), activity of the electron transport chain, ROS generation, and susceptibility to mitochondrial permeability transition pore opening (Lesnefsky et al., 2016; Boengler et al., 2017).
